title: PAC learning of finite automata under the uniform distribution
formal: Are deterministic finite automata efficiently PAC learnable from independent uniformly distributed words and their acceptance bits? Use the ordinary finite-word, fixed-length uniform model. Does there exist one randomized classical Turing machine \(L\) and one polynomial \(p\) such that, for every alphabet size \(q\ge2\), word length \(n\ge1\), state bound \(s\ge1\), integers \(a,b\ge3\), and deterministic finite automaton \(M\) with at most \(s\) states over \(\Sigma_q=\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\), the following holds? Given \(1^q,1^n,1^s,1^a,1^b\) and access only to independent examples \((w,M(w))\) with \(w\sim U_{q,n}\), \(L\) runs in worst-case time at most \(p(q+n+s+a+b)\), and outputs a finite predictor \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr_{L,\,\mathrm{examples}}\left[\Pr_{w\sim U_{q,n}}[h(w)\ne M(w)]\le\frac1a\right]\ge1-\frac1b?\] The predictor may use any efficiently evaluable representation; it need not be an automaton. A 2021 theorem rules out this guarantee under a specified local-pseudorandom-generator assumption, already for binary alphabets. This card retains the unconditional algorithm-existence question, while recording that published conditional negative answer explicitly.

source_formulation.text: Can deterministic finite automata be PAC learned efficiently under uniformly distributed words?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

why: Finite-state machines give very small descriptions of potentially complicated behavior on long strings. This question isolates whether uniformly random training words make that behavior computationally learnable from acceptance labels alone. It separates the simplicity of the sampling distribution from the difficulty of recovering a useful predictor.
status_note: The 2019 source’s open-status sentence predates Daniely–Vardi (COLT 2021), whose Theorem 12 gives a conditional negative answer under Assumption 1 on local pseudorandom generators, already for weak improper learning over the uniform Boolean hypercube. The official ALT 2026 Table 1 retains that premise. These full primary statements were checked on 16 September 2026. The card preserves the unconditional existence question and therefore remains active with uncertain unconditional status; the assumption is neither silently adopted nor asserted proved. Bounded checks found no unconditional matching resolution.

progress.text: The original source attributes the ordinary-DFA uniform-distribution PAC question to Pitt and distinguishes it from active-query learning.
Angluin–Chen obtain a positive result for random transition graphs with terminal-state information, a stronger observation interface than binary acceptance labels.
Daniely–Vardi Theorem 12 rules out even inverse-polynomial-advantage improper weak learning on the uniform Boolean hypercube under their local-PRG Assumption 1.
The ALT regular-expression paper’s Table 1 explicitly cites the local-PRG-dependent uniform DFA hardness, separate from its own regular-expression results.

Checked the original DFA and finite-word uniform definitions, the full 2021 learning model and assumption/theorem, and the official 2026 table. The conditional negative answer is recorded without converting it into an unconditional archival resolution.

category_assignment.reason: The retained question is PAC learnability of finite automata, not their representation or equivalence.

importance.reason: A classical computational-learning question about a basic representation class. The later conditional hardness on the uniform hypercube is a major clarification, and the distinctions between random examples, active queries, hidden-state information and improper prediction are fundamental.

sentences: The card asks whether every finite automaton can be learned efficiently from uniformly sampled words labeled only by acceptance.
The learner knows the word length, alphabet and state bound and may return any efficient predictor.
It must achieve every requested accuracy and confidence using polynomial time without membership queries or state information.
A published local-pseudorandom-generator assumption rules out even weak improper learning on uniform binary words, and a 2026 source retains that premise.
The completed card records this conditional negative answer while preserving the original unconditional question and its exact Lean decision criterion.

definitions:
A deterministic finite automaton is a tuple \(M=(\Sigma_q,Q,q_0,F,\tau)\) with a nonempty finite state set \(Q\), \(|Q|\le s\), initial state \(q_0\in Q\), accepting states \(F\subseteq Q\), and a total transition function \(\tau:Q\times\Sigma_q\to Q\). Starting at \(q_0\), it reads the letters of a finite word from left to right and updates its current state by \(\tau\); \(M(w)=1\) exactly when its final state lies in \(F\), and otherwise \(M(w)=0\). The target transition table, states and accepting set are hidden. The public value \(s\) is an upper bound on the number of states, not the full target description. The source’s size convention is state count. A complete transition-table encoding has length polynomial in \(s\) and \(q\), so the explicit polynomial dependence on both parameters accounts for that representation.

\(U_{q,n}\) assigns probability \(q^{-n}\) to every word in \(\Sigma_q^n\); equivalently its \(n\) letters are independent and uniform in \(\Sigma_q\). Each oracle request supplies a fresh independent word and its deterministic acceptance bit under the same fixed \(M\). The learner may request more independent examples adaptively but cannot select the word to be labeled. It sees neither the final state nor the sequence of intermediate states. There are no membership queries, equivalence queries, counterexamples, nonuniform advice or random-target assumption. The guarantee must hold for every automaton, including arbitrarily chosen transition graphs and accepting sets. Randomness in the outer probability comes only from examples and the learner’s independent fair coins; the inner probability is error on a fresh uniform word. This is the realizable PAC model with noiseless labels. Parameters \(1/a\) and \(1/b\) range over inverse integers, which suffice to express every desired positive accuracy and failure tolerance by rounding downward.

For a concrete hypothesis interface, encode each letter in \(\lceil\log_2 q\rceil\) bits and let the output be an ordinary Boolean circuit on the resulting \(n\lceil\log_2 q\rceil\) bits. Its output on valid word encodings is \(h(w)\); values on unused letter codes are irrelevant. The circuit may use two-input AND/OR, one-input NOT and constant gates with a fixed effective binary encoding. Its description is written within the learning-time bound and is evaluated without examples or access to the target. This expresses unrestricted improper efficient prediction: the output is not constrained to at most \(s\) states or to a minimal consistent automaton. Uniformly polynomial-time evaluable finite predictors have ordinary polynomial-size circuit representations under the usual bit-computation convention. All bit operations, reading examples, fair random bits and output writing count toward the one polynomial bound, as does the number of example requests. The example oracle supplies the promised distribution; its own sampling computation is not charged. The same machine and polynomial work for all displayed parameters, lengths and targets.

Uniformity refers to words of the specified length, not to an impossible probability measure assigning equal mass to all of \(\Sigma_q^*\). The learner may depend on the public \(n\), and its guarantee is only over words of that length. Exact identification of the complete infinite regular language, prediction simultaneously at every length by one output, geometric length mixtures, and real-valued limit-average behavior on infinite words are different tasks. The arbitrary-finite-alphabet convention follows the source’s DFA and \(U^n\) definitions; the later hardness theorem applies already when \(q=2\). Computational efficiency is essential: the question does not merely ask for a finite or polynomial information-theoretic sample bound.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of \(L,p\) with the complete uniform guarantee in Lean, or prove its logical negation: for every proposed machine and polynomial, some allowed parameters and target violate the runtime, finite-output or PAC condition. A positive answer must allow every target automaton and observe only independent acceptance-labeled uniform words. A result for random transition graphs, additional state labels, membership queries or only a fixed bounded state count does not meet the statement. A negative answer under the local-PRG assumption is a conditional theorem and must retain that premise; it does not by itself prove the unconditional negation. Hardness of finding a smallest consistent DFA also does not exclude an arbitrary efficient predictor. The yes/no assertion has exact logical quantifiers and rational error/confidence tolerances; no numerical optimum is being approximated.

context_blocks.text: The 2019 source studies weighted limit-average automata, but its related-work paragraph cites Pitt’s older question about ordinary deterministic automata. The imported card refers to that ordinary Boolean acceptance problem. The paper’s own infinite-word impossibility and minimization results concern a different model and do not answer the selected question.

Knowing that every finite automaton has a finite transition table does not imply a polynomial learning algorithm. There are only finitely many targets at a fixed state bound, but computationally finding a useful predictor is a stronger requirement than having enough examples to identify one statistically. The target permits improper prediction and therefore does not ask for minimum-state reconstruction.

Daniely–Vardi Theorem 12 proves a conditional obstruction substantially stronger than failure of high-accuracy PAC learning: for every constants c, η>0, no efficient learner achieves error at most 1/2−1/n^c for all n^η-state DFAs under the uniform distribution on n-bit words, under their Assumption 1. The learning model allows arbitrary efficiently evaluable hypotheses. Consequently the obstruction is not merely a lower bound for proper automaton reconstruction.

Assumption 1 is the existence of Goldreich-style local pseudorandom generators with every constant polynomial stretch: for each constant \(t>1\), some constant locality \(k\) and Boolean predicate \(P\) make the length-\(N^t\) output formed by applying \(P\) to independent random ordered \(k\)-tuples of distinct seed positions computationally indistinguishable from uniform with advantage at most \(1/3\). The chosen tuples are public to the polynomial-time distinguisher. This is an unproved computational assumption, not a consequence of merely defining a finite automaton or a uniform distribution. The exact security convention is the named Assumption 1 of the cited paper; it is not added as a premise of this card’s unconditional target.

The official ALT 2026 paper on learning regular expressions explicitly lists uniform-distribution DFA PAC hardness under its local-PRG Assumption C and attributes that result to Daniely–Vardi. Its additional regular-expression results concern a different succinct representation: equivalent languages can require exponentially different description sizes. Thus the 2026 table corroborates the conditional status rather than proving the cryptographic premise.

Angluin–Chen’s 2015 positive result assumes a random transition graph and access to information about the terminal state reached by a sampled word. The acceptance bit does not identify that state. Likewise, the known polynomial algorithms with membership and equivalence queries use more information than the sampling-only oracle in this card. These distinctions prevent positive results in richer observation models from being substituted for the target.

The historical source described the question as open in 2019; that summary is incomplete after the 2021 conditional hardness theorem. The present record makes this development prominent and keeps current unconditional status uncertain. It does not claim that an unproved local-PRG assumption has been established or that a bounded literature check proves continued unconditional openness.
